catalog_quote: Una característica importante del quechua es la acentuación grave de casi todas las palabras, de tal modo que los acentos ortográficos no son necesarios. Empero, en [a]quellas con acento agudo, que son excepciones a la regla [ge]neral, se utiliza el acento ortográfico. Se debe notar que cuando una determinada partícula [se] elimina (es decir, cuando no se pronuncia algunos sufijos), [el] acento se queda en la sílaba precedente al sufijo [el]iminado, y puesto que en este caso el acento es agudo, se representa ortográficamente. Ejemplos: Wasita munani (tiene acento en la penúltima sílaba) ... Imátaq sutin (tiene acento el la penúltima sílaba) ... Pero: Wasí munani (tiene acento en la última sílaba pues se eliminó el sufijo -ta) Imá sutiyki (tiene acento en la última sílaba, pues se eliminó el sufijo -taq) ... Por otra parte, el sufijo -chá (dubitativo, indica duda), [o]cupa siempre la últ…

new_statements.quote: En el QT el acento generalmente ocurre en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra. Sí a la palabra se le añaden más sufijos, el acento recorre a la penúltima sílaba (Plaza 2009), ver (87). El acento en quechua se caracteriza por notarse en la prosodia, es decir la pronunciación, y no así en la escritura. [...] Las excepciones a la acentuación prosódica de la penúltima sílaba de la palabra ocurren en los siguientes casos: a) El acento se expresa ortográficamente en la última sílaba de la palabra cuando se expresa dirección (Stark, Segovia, & Segovia 1971), ver (89).
new_statements.translation: In Tarabuco Quechua (QT) the accent generally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. If more suffixes are added to the word, the accent moves along to the penultimate syllable (Plaza 2009), see (87). Accent in Quechua is characterized by being noticed in the prosody, i.e. in pronunciation, and not in writing. [...] The exceptions to prosodic accentuation of the penultimate syllable of the word occur in the following cases: a) The accent is expressed orthographically on the last syllable of the word when address is expressed (Stark, Segovia & Segovia 1971), see (89).
new_statements.citation: Vargas Melgarejo, Gaby Gabriela. 2023. Fonología del quechua de Tarabuco. Thesis, 95 pp. (Glottolog ref 687750)
new_statements.locator: §2.5 'El acento', printed pp. 88-90 (PDF pp. 89-91); University of Arizona MA thesis (hdl 10150/668305), downloaded as the Internet Archive copy of the UA repository bitstream because repository.arizona.edu could not be reached by automated download and the listed the Harvard library catalogue/ProQuest link is login-only
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate = penultimate stress); adds the exception list and the observation that the position moves with suffixation. Describes the Tarabuco (Chuquisaca) variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable and shifts rightward as suffixes are added (llaqta > llaqta-KA-ma > llaqta-ka-MA-lla). Final stress arises only in a closed list of cases.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in: (a) address/vocative forms (tatáy 'father!' vs. tátay 'my father'); (b) exclamations (atatáy, alaláw, wáy); (c) omission of the accusative -ta or emphatic -taq, leaving the stem finally stressed (wasí muna-ni 'I want a house'); (d) apocope of words/suffixes (ari > á, icharí > í, mana > má, -manta > -mán, -chus > -s); (e) arí 'yes' vs. ári 'well then' as a stress minimal pair; (f) inherently final-stressed suffixes -chá (conjectural), -má (surprisive), -rí (emphatic/connective); (g) onomatopoeia (laq'áq). pp. 88-90.
new_statements.identity_note: Vargas Melgarejo 2023 describes the Quechua of Tarabuco (Chuquisaca department), which she places within Bolivian Southern Quechua [quh]. Camacho Rios 2022 describes the speech of monolingual elders of Uma Piwra (Cochabamba), 'UPSBQ', and notes that the -rpa-n final-stress case is not common in standard SBQ. Sola & Lastra 1964 (and Lastra 1968) describe Cochabamba Quechua. The SPA 1979 sheet (entry 895) is also Cochabamba, built on Bills et al. 1969 and Lastra 1968. All are South Bolivian Quechua varieties; no source claims a different placement for any of them.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Southern Quechua is penultimate (Parker 1965, Adelaar 1984 y Palomino 1993). Similar statements have been made for South Bolivian Quechua (Bills G., et al 1971, Herrero & Sanchez 1978). Although, Plaza (2009:223) remarks on some exceptions to this penultimate default system. UPSBQ marks pitch accent in two ways: penultimate and final. The core stress is realized on the penultimate syllable. The second type corresponds to pitch accent in final syllable. This last one can be sub-divided into two: a phonemic final stress conditioned by certain morphemes that attract the pitch accent and a final stress conditioned by final suffix deletion rule.
new_statements.citation: Camacho Rios, Gladys. 2022. Verbal Complexity in South Bolivian Quechua: Insights from the Speech of Monolingual Elders. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin. 296 pp.
new_statements.locator: §3.3.4 'Stress', pp. 65-67 (PDF pages = printed pages); §3.4.1 'Suffix deletion rule', p. 68ff; summary statement also §3.3.1 p. 61 ('The default stress system is penultimate, but the natural speech of elders also shows final stress assignment triggered by a suffix deletion rule'). downloaded from CORE (core.ac.uk/download/, harvested from Texas ScholarWorks) because the DOI target repositories.lib.utexas.edu could not be reached by automated download
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's penultimate placement and adds morphologically conditioned final-stress exceptions plus the phrase-level note. The author calls the phenomenon 'pitch accent' in places but treats it as the stress system (section titled 'Stress'); this is a terminological choice, not a claim that the language lacks word stress. Variety: Uma Piwra (Cochabamba) monolingual elders' speech (UPSBQ).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default (core) stress on the penultimate syllable of the word, shown for nouns, verbs and at phrase level (máki, wállpa, pilipíntu, puríni, qarásun); final stress only when a stress-attracting enclitic is present or a final suffix has been deleted.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Explicitly left open: 'Primary stress, secondary stress and intonation at a phrase level are still unexplored.' (p. 65).
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics =chá (dubitative/evidential) and =rí (interrogative) inherently bear the pitch accent, giving final stress (pp. 65-67, Figures 3-4); the suffix -rpa 'suddenly' + -n (3SG) yields a heavy CCVC final syllable that attracts stress (sarurpán, wayk'urpán), 'not common in standard SBQ' (p. 67); a monosyllabic suffix deletion rule (accusative -ta, topic =qa, negative mana) leaves the stress on what is now the final syllable (p. 68).
new_statements.identity_note: Vargas Melgarejo 2023 describes the Quechua of Tarabuco (Chuquisaca department), which she places within Bolivian Southern Quechua [quh]. Camacho Rios 2022 describes the speech of monolingual elders of Uma Piwra (Cochabamba), 'UPSBQ', and notes that the -rpa-n final-stress case is not common in standard SBQ. Sola & Lastra 1964 (and Lastra 1968) describe Cochabamba Quechua. The SPA 1979 sheet (entry 895) is also Cochabamba, built on Bills et al. 1969 and Lastra 1968. All are South Bolivian Quechua varieties; no source claims a different placement for any of them.

new_statements.quote: [Sola & Lastra 1964, p. 7, scanned verbatim] 2.3 Stress and Juncture. The stress contrast of Cochabamba Quechua involves two significant levels, strong and weak. Weak stress has two allophones, the stronger of the two occurring on checked syllables. Strong stress is marked by the acute diacritic, or by space if no diacritic is written. In the latter case strong stress occurs on the penultimate Syllable before space, and, in words of more than four syViables; a the first syllable after the space. [scanned: 'syllables, on'] [p. 4:] stress merks [marks] are omitted unless the stress falls on a syllable other than the penultimate in words of more than one syllable; they are also omitted in monosyllables.
new_statements.citation: Lastra, Yolanda. 1968. Cochabamba Quechua Syntax (Janua Linguarum, Series Practica 40). The Hague: Mouton. Ch. 1 'Phonology'.

Deciding passage: §2.3 'Stress and Juncture', printed p. 7 (PDF p. 11); notation statement p. 4 (PDF p. 8); accusative allomorph p. 25
new_statements.relation_note: Penultimate placement agrees with the catalog; adds an initial secondary stress in longer words, the phonemic status of stress, and suffixal final-stress allomorphs. Caveat: this is the 1964 ERIC precursor, not the 1968 Mouton text; the SPA 1979 sheet held by the project cites Lastra 1968 pp. 12-19 for the phonology, consistent with the same analysis. Variety: Cochabamba Quechua.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Strong (primary) stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (word = the stretch between spaces); in words of more than four syllables a second strong stress on the first syllable. Stress is treated as a phoneme (two contrastive levels) because some suffix allomorphs consist of stress alone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words of more than four syllables carry strong stress on the initial syllable as well as on the penult (p. 7); weak stress is stronger on checked syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress written only when it is non-penultimate (p. 4). The accusative -ta has an allomorph consisting of stress on the last syllable of the substantive, in free variation with -ta when the noun is not phrase-final (p. 25); the dubitative -chus likewise has a stress allomorph in word-final position (morphology chapter).

sources.quote: "En general, el acento es penúltimo en la palabra —por ejemplo, kusikúni 'estoy feliz'—, pero algunos sufijos finales requieren un acento final —por ejemplo, ¿qamrí? '¿y tú?'—. El acento también puede ser final en el caso que el morfema acusativo -ta se elide —por ejemplo, papá 'papa, acusativo' en contraste con papáta 'papa, acusativo' (Camacho Rios, 2023)—, o para indicar un sentido discursivo aún no bien entendido —por ejemplo, nuqáqa y nuqaqá 'yo, tópico'—."
sources.locator: p. 76, sec. 2 (background on SBQ phonology); also p. 86 Tabla 3b
